# NVIDIA GPU Market: Rental Rates Fluctuate, Prices Surge, Depreciation

 August 4, 2026 · 02:01 UTC Add GG Echo as a preferred source on Google 

 Sarah Lin Corporate Watchdog & Business Analyst B.S. Economics & Corporate Finance 

Alright, this convention floor is a madhouse, but the data is coming in, and it’s a mess, just like my brain right now. Okay, so the big story, the one everyone’s whispering about, is this whole GPU depreciation thing, right? The original article from Wccftech, it was talking about how A100, H100, H200 rental rates were pricing upwards, and B200s were just shy of $6 an hour. That was August 3, 2026. But here’s the thing, the market is moving fast, really fast. Some of the newer data, like from Q2 2026, actually shows H100 cloud rental rates fell from around $8 an hour in early 2023 to $1.80-$3.50 an hour.

Spot pricing even hit $1.20 an hour. That’s a pretty big drop, not exactly “pricing upwards” across the board for everything. B200s, the new hotness, their rental rates in Q2 2026 are sitting around $4.50-$7.00 an hour. So that “just shy of $6” from the Wccftech article, it’s still in the ballpark, but it’s a range now, and some providers are even lower. Vast.ai, for example, lists B200s at $4.38 an hour.

Runcrate even has B200 cloud rental from $3.20 an hour. GPUs.io shows a market median of $6.03 an hour across 20 configurations for B200s. So, it’s not a single upward trajectory for all GPUs, and the B200 is definitely seeing some competitive pricing. The H200, which is supposed to bridge the gap between H100 and B200, is going for about $3.00-$4.50 an hour in Q2 2026. Thunder Compute has H100 80GB at $2.19 an hour, and A100 80GB at $1.09 an hour as of August 2, 2026.

Major cloud providers like AWS have cut costs for H100, H200, and A100 instances by up to 45%. This is creating opportunities for developers who were priced out before. The depreciation argument, that’s still a huge deal. Proponents of a longer shelf life, they say these GPUs are useful for more than the traditional 3-year estimate. The rising rental rates for some older GPUs, like the A100s and H100s, earlier in the year, that was bolstering the longer useful life argument.

But then you see the H100 rates falling in Q2 2026. It’s a mixed signal. Michael Burry, remember him, he accused hyperscalers in November 2025 of accounting manipulation, saying they depreciate NVIDIA GPUs over five to six years when the real economic life is closer to two or three. He thinks this could lead to $176 billion in understated depreciation and overstated profits between 2026 and 2028. That’s a massive number, and it makes you think about the true value of these assets over time. The global AI compute market is projected to be over $700 billion in capital expenditures this year alone, targeting high-performance GPUs and custom ASICs.

The GPU rental market is projected to grow from $3.34 billion in 2023 to $26.09 billion by 2032. That’s huge growth, but the question is, how much of that is sustainable, and how much is just a race to build out infrastructure that might become obsolete faster than expected?NVIDIA still dominates the AI accelerator market, holding an estimated 75% to 81% of AI accelerator revenue in 2026. Their data center revenue for the quarter ended April 26, 2026, was $75.2 billion, up 92% year over year. That’s just insane growth.

But AMD’s MI300X is out there, with rental pricing approximately 30-40 percent below H100 for comparable inference performance. The software ecosystem, ROCm, is still the differentiator there. The memory crisis is real too. HBM demand has outstripped supply. An H100 uses 80 GB of HBM3, the H200 uses 141 GB of HBM3E, and the B200 needs 192 GB of HBM3E.

Micron projects the HBM total addressable market at $35 billion for calendar 2025, growing to approximately $100 billion by 2028. Micron and SK Hynix have stated their HBM capacity through 2026 is fully booked or sold out. This memory shortage definitely impacts GPU availability and pricing. And get this, NVIDIA is reportedly planning to raise GPU prices by another 20% to 30%. This isn’t just for flagship models, it could affect their consumer lineup too.

Some board partners have already pushed prices higher in certain regions, like in China, where RTX 50-series GPU prices have increased by as much as 20%. The RTX 5090, which launched at $1,999, has been selling for as much as $4,500. That’s just wild. So, while some rental rates are actually coming down due to increased supply and competition, like for H100s, the overall picture for GPU pricing, especially for new hardware and consumer cards, seems to be heading up. It’s a weird dichotomy, right?My personal trade, I bought NVDA back on January 15, 2021, at $12.81 a share.

I’m holding that until it hits $300 or I need to pay for my kid’s college, whichever comes first. The next earnings report for NVDA is expected on August 26, 2026. The useful life debate, it’s critical. Hyperscalers follow a 3-4 year amortization cycle for GPUs, but some neoclouds are using a 6-year depreciation. If the economic life is shorter, those balance sheets are going to look a lot different.

The global data center GPU market is projected to grow from $138.88 billion in 2026 to $624.17 billion by 2034. That’s a lot of hardware to depreciate.
